label: Decide if a sentence is a proposition
subgoals: Test for a declarative sentence form
Check it has one definite truth value

slice.rule: A proposition is a declarative sentence that has one definite truth value: it is either true or false, and there is no third option. A question or a command is not a proposition, because it asserts nothing for a truth value to attach to. A sentence that looks declarative but leaves its truth unsettled — *this number is large* — is not a proposition either.

examples.item: The Moon is made of green cheese.

examples.says: a question, so not a proposition
a command, so not a proposition

slice.note: A false statement is a proposition. Only statements with no truth value at all are rejected.

label: Sort true, false, and non-propositions
subgoals: Flag vague open sentences like x is large
Count propositions in a mixed list

slice.rule: Sort in two passes. First ask whether the sentence asserts anything: a question or command goes straight out. Then, for whatever is left, decide whether it is true or false. That second step never changes the category — it only assigns a value — so a false statement stays a proposition.

examples.says: asserts something, so a proposition, and it is false
a request, so not a proposition
a question, so not a proposition

label: Apply the proposition test at speed
subgoals: Name the disqualifier for each reject

slice.rule: Run one pass over a mixed list. For each sentence ask only: does this assert something with a definite truth value? Reject questions, commands and requests on sight, and reject anything whose truth value is genuinely unsettled. When you reject one, name the disqualifier rather than leaving the reason implicit.

examples.says: declarative with a definite value — kept

slice.note: Naming the disqualifier is most of the work: a rejection without a reason is not a decision yet.
